title: The change control process
blurb: Explain the purpose and importance of each change control stage, in order, and what goes wrong when one is skipped.
question: Eight months into the Millbrook Station upgrade, the train operator asks for a lift to platform 2. The site team offers to 'just get on with it'. Which stages should the request pass through, in what order, and why does each stage matter?

teach.body: Change control is the process through which every request to change the approved baseline is captured, evaluated and then approved, rejected or deferred. In plain English: nothing alters the agreed plan until someone with the right authority has seen what the change really involves and said yes. Its purpose is not to stop change. It protects the baseline and the business case, prevents scope creep, and makes sure worthwhile changes happen in a controlled, visible way.

steps.label: Request
steps.sub: Raised and logged in the change log

steps.label:

evaluation
steps.sub: Quick screen: worth a full assessment?

steps.label:
Detailed
evaluation
steps.sub: Impact on scope, time, cost, quality, risk, benefits

steps.label: Recommendation
steps.sub: Approve, reject or defer; right authority decides

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: Make the change and communicate it

teach.caption: Six stages, always in this order. There is no 'review' or 'monitor' stage: update plans comes before implement.

teach.h: Really Important Decisions Require Updated Information
teach.word: R I D R U I
teach.caption: Small look before big look (initial, then detailed). Paper before work (update plans, then implement).

teach.body: Millbrook Station is being upgraded under a linear life cycle; its design and budget were baselined at the end of definition. In month 8 the train operator's accessibility lead asks for a lift to platform 2 so the whole station is step-free. The site manager offers to start digging straight away. Instead, the project manager logs the request as CR-031 and takes it through change control. The change control lessons in this section all follow CR-031.

head: Stage
Purpose
Why it matters
rows: Nothing is lost; audit trail starts
teach.caption: In a written answer, 'purpose' is what the stage does; 'importance' is what it protects or prevents.

teach.h: Two evaluations, two levels of effort
teach.body: Detailed evaluation is expensive: engineers, cost consultants and the scheduler all spend time on it. The initial evaluation is a quick, proportionate filter that stops that effort being wasted on duplicates, requests that clash with the objectives, or trivial items. For CR-031 the PM's initial view is that a lift supports the business case's accessibility objective, so it is worth a full look. The detailed evaluation then works out the real impact before anyone recommends a decision.

teach.caption: Only an approved change reaches update plans and implement. Every outcome is recorded in the change log.

teach.h: What goes wrong if a stage is skipped
head: Skip this
Likely consequence
rows: Specialist time wasted on poor ideas
Work to old plans; false variances
Change not delivered or not known
teach.caption: This is the 'importance' half of the outcome. Exam scenarios often describe a skipped stage and ask for the consequence.

teach.text: Three order traps. Initial evaluation always comes BEFORE detailed evaluation. Update plans always comes BEFORE implement. And there is no 'review', 'monitor' or 'close' stage in the six: if an option lists one, it is wrong. Also note who decides: the project manager makes the recommendation, but the decision belongs to the appropriate authority (often the sponsor) unless the change is within the PM's delegated limits.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the stages in order: request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans, implement.
For each stage asked about, state its purpose in one clause (what it does).
Then state its importance (what it protects: baseline, business case, effort, authority).
Use a mini example, e.g. 'a request for an extra lift is logged with a unique reference'.
Close with the overall point: changes are made deliberately, not by drift.
Change control protects the baseline and business case; it does not exist to block change.
Order: request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans, implement.
Initial evaluation is a quick screen; detailed evaluation assesses the full impact and options.
The appropriate authority approves, rejects or defers, and the outcome is recorded.
Plans and records are updated before the change is implemented and communicated.

summary: You can now name the six stages of a typical change control process in order and explain the purpose and importance of each. You can also predict what goes wrong when a stage is skipped, which is how the exam usually tests it.

A.q: What is the main purpose of the initial evaluation stage of change control?
options: To decide if a full assessment is needed
To work out the full cost and time impacts
To make the final decision on the change
To issue revised plans to the whole team
A.why: Initial evaluation is a quick, proportionate screen that decides whether a request deserves the effort of a detailed evaluation.

whyNot.1: Working out the full impact is the detailed evaluation, which comes next.
whyNot.2: The decision is made at the recommendation stage, by the appropriate authority.
whyNot.3: Revised plans are issued at the update plans stage, after approval.

A.q: In a typical change control process, which stage comes immediately before 'implement'?
options: Recommendation
Update plans
Detailed evaluation
Review and monitor
A.why: Once a change is approved, the plans, baseline and configuration records are updated, and only then is the change implemented.

whyNot.0: Recommendation comes before update plans, not directly before implement.
whyNot.2: Detailed evaluation is the third stage, well before implementation.
whyNot.3: 'Review and monitor' is not one of the six change control stages.

A.q: Why should a change request be logged as soon as it is raised?
options: So the team can begin the work early
So the sponsor approves it at once
So it is tracked and never lost
So the baseline is updated at once
A.why: Logging gives the request a reference and a status, so it can be tracked through to a decision and an audit trail starts.

whyNot.0: No work should start until the change has been evaluated and approved.
whyNot.1: Logging does not trigger approval; the request still has to be evaluated.
whyNot.3: The baseline only changes at the update plans stage, after approval.

B.q: For CR-031, the project manager asks the structural engineer and cost consultant to work out what a platform 2 lift would add to cost, time and risk. Which stage is this?
options: Request
Initial evaluation
Recommendation
Detailed evaluation
B.why: Detailed evaluation uses specialists to assess the full impact of the change on scope, time, cost, quality, risk and benefits.

whyNot.0: The request stage only raises and logs the change.
whyNot.1: Initial evaluation is a quick screen, not a specialist impact assessment.
whyNot.2: Recommendation uses the results of this assessment to approve, reject or defer.

B.q: What is the main reason for updating plans BEFORE an approved change is implemented?
options: Everyone then works to the same baseline
It allows the sponsor to undo the decision
It removes the need to tell stakeholders
It closes the request in the change log
B.why: Updating plans first means the team builds from current plans and progress is measured against a baseline that includes the change.

whyNot.1: Updating plans puts the decision into effect; it is not a chance to reverse it.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders still need to be told; implementation includes communicating the change.
whyNot.3: The request is closed once the change has been implemented, not when plans are updated.

B.q: Which of the following is NOT a stage in a typical change control process?
options: Initial evaluation
Recommendation
Review and monitor
Update plans
B.why: The six stages are request, initial evaluation, detailed evaluation, recommendation, update plans and implement. 'Review and monitor' is not one of them.

whyNot.0: Initial evaluation is the second stage.
whyNot.3: Update plans is the fifth stage.

C.q: Hearing that the operator wants a lift, Millbrook's site manager starts excavating a lift shaft the same day 'to save time'. What is the most significant consequence?
options: The change log becomes too long to manage
Work is done that nobody assessed or agreed
The operator loses the right to ask for change
The business case no longer needs reviewing
C.why: Skipping evaluation and recommendation means cost, time and risk are unknown and no one with authority has agreed the change: uncontrolled scope change.

whyNot.0: Log length is an admin matter; the real problem is unassessed, unauthorised work.
whyNot.2: Stakeholders keep the right to request changes; that is what the process is for.
whyNot.3: A significant change makes a business case review more important, not less.

C.q: Which THREE are purposes of the detailed evaluation stage? 1. Assess the impact on cost and time 2. Assess the effect on benefits 3. Give the request a unique reference 4. Identify the effect on risk
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
1, 2 and 4
C.why: Detailed evaluation assesses impact on cost and time (1), benefits and the business case (2) and risk (4). The unique reference (3) is given when the request is raised and logged.

whyNot.0: Giving a reference (3) happens at the request stage, not detailed evaluation.
whyNot.1: Giving a reference (3) happens at the request stage, and this misses benefits (2).
whyNot.2: Giving a reference (3) happens at the request stage, and this misses cost and time (1).

C.q: A request to change the colour of Millbrook's waiting-room seats is raised. The PM's quick check shows it repeats a request rejected last month for having no benefit, with nothing new added. What should happen?
options: Close it at initial evaluation, noting why
Send it on for a full detailed evaluation
Approve it, as the cost is likely to be low
Update the plans so it can be built later
C.why: Initial evaluation exists to filter out requests not worth a full assessment, such as duplicates with no new information. The reason is recorded and the requester told.

whyNot.1: A full assessment would waste specialist effort on a request already judged to have no benefit.
whyNot.2: Low cost is not a justification; it has no benefit and has not been properly decided.
whyNot.3: Plans are only updated for approved changes.

reteach.title: Think of a wedding
reteach.question: The venue, menu and guest list are all booked. A month before the day, the groom's mother asks to add a live band. What should the couple do before anyone books one?

blocks.h: The same six stages, at a wedding
blocks.body: The request is written on the planning list so it is not forgotten. A quick check: is there even space for a band? If so, a proper look: band fee, extra power, a later finish, noise rules, and whether it is worth it. The couple, who hold the budget, decide yes, no or 'maybe for the evening party'. If yes, the timetable, budget and venue booking are updated first. Then the band is booked and everyone is told.

steps.label:
Detailed
evaluation
steps.sub: Fee, power, finish time, worth it?

blocks.text: If the band were booked before the venue booking and timetable were updated, they could turn up to find no power and a 10 pm curfew. That is why update plans comes before implement.

explain.body: Any stakeholder can raise a change request through the agreed route. It is logged in the change log with a unique reference so it is tracked and visible. The initial evaluation is a quick screen: does it fit the objectives, is it a duplicate, and is it worth the effort of a full assessment?

test.q: Who can usually raise a change request on a project?
options: Only the project sponsor
Only the project manager
Any stakeholder, via the agreed route
Only the supplier's commercial manager
test.why: Changes can come from anyone with an interest in the project, so any stakeholder can raise a request, as long as it goes through the agreed route and is logged.

whyNot.0: The sponsor can raise requests, but so can other stakeholders.
whyNot.1: The PM manages the process but is not the only person who can raise a request.
whyNot.3: Suppliers can raise requests, but they are not the only ones who can.

explain.body: A thorough look at the options and the impact on scope, time, cost, quality, risk, benefits and the business case. Specialists and configuration records help. Its importance: the decision that follows rests on evidence, not on who shouts loudest.

test.q: Why must the detailed evaluation be completed before a recommendation is made?
options: So the requester can change their mind
So the plans can be rebaselined early
So the work can start during the evaluation
So the decision rests on the full impact
test.why: Without a full understanding of the impact, approve, reject or defer would be a guess; the evaluation gives the decision-maker the evidence.

whyNot.0: Requesters can withdraw at any time; that is not why the order matters.
whyNot.1: Plans are rebaselined only after approval, at the update plans stage.
whyNot.2: No work should start until the change is approved and the plans updated.

explain.body: Using the evaluation, the project manager recommends approve, reject or defer, justified against the business case. The decision is taken by the appropriate authority, often the sponsor or a change board, unless the change is within the PM's delegated limits. The decision and its reasons are recorded and the requester is told.

test.q: Which list gives the three possible outcomes at the recommendation stage?
options: Approve, escalate or close
Approve, reject or defer
Accept, transfer or reject
Approve, implement or log
test.why: A change is approved, rejected or deferred at the recommendation stage.

whyNot.0: Escalate and close are not the three change decisions.
whyNot.2: Accept and transfer are risk responses, not change decisions.
whyNot.3: Implement and log are other parts of the process, not decisions.

explain.body: An approved change first updates the baseline, the project management plan and the configuration records, so everyone works to one current version. Then it is implemented: the work is done and the change and its effects are communicated to everyone affected.

steps.label: Implement
steps.sub: Do the work and communicate it

test.q: Besides carrying out the work, what does the implement stage include?
options: Re-running the initial evaluation
Raising a fresh change request
Telling those affected about the change
Deciding whether the change is approved
test.why: Implementation means making the change and communicating it and its effects to the stakeholders it affects.

whyNot.0: The evaluations are finished before the decision is made.
whyNot.1: The change has already been requested and approved.
whyNot.3: The approval decision was made at the recommendation stage.
